q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂Cl is:
x: CH₃CH₂Cl has a two-carbon chain (ethane) with one chlorine, so it is chloroethane (common name ethyl chloride).

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CHBrCH₃ is:
x: The chain has three carbons with Br on the middle carbon, so it is 2-bromopropane. 1-Bromopropane is CH₃CH₂CH₂Br, its positional isomer.

q: The IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CCl is:
x: The longest chain is three carbons (propane); C-2 carries both a methyl group and the chlorine, giving 2-chloro-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl chloride).

q: CHCl₃, commonly called chloroform, has the IUPAC name:
x: CHCl₃ is methane with three H atoms replaced by Cl, so it is trichloromethane. Tetrachloromethane is CCl₄.

q: Which of the following is a secondary alkyl halide?
x: In 2-bromobutane the carbon bearing Br is attached to two other carbons, so it is secondary. 1-Bromobutane is primary and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is tertiary.

q: 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane, CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)₂Cl, is classified as a:
x: The carbon carrying Cl is bonded to three other carbon atoms (two methyls and an ethyl), so the alkyl halide is tertiary.

q: The condensed formula of 1-bromo-2-methylpropane is:
x: Propane chain with Br on C-1 and a methyl on C-2 gives BrCH₂CH(CH₃)CH₃, i.e. (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br. (CH₃)₃CBr is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

q: How many structural isomers are possible for the alkyl halide C₄H₉Br?
x: There are four: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. Two come from the straight chain and two from the branched chain.

q: The IUPAC name of BrCH₂CH₂Br is:
x: There are two carbons, each carrying one Br, so the name is 1,2-dibromoethane. 1,1-Dibromoethane would be CH₃CHBr₂.

q: The correct IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(Cl)CH₃ is:
x: The longest chain has five carbons. Numbering from either end gives locants 2 and 4, so the tie is broken alphabetically: chloro comes before methyl and gets the lower number, giving 2-chloro-4-methylpentane.

q: The general formula of a monohaloalkane (alkyl halide) is:
x: An alkyl group is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁, so an alkyl halide is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X, formed by replacing one H of an alkane CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with a halogen.

q: In the C–X bond of an alkyl halide, the carbon atom carries:
o: No charge, as the bond is non-polar
x: The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls the bonding electrons towards itself. Carbon becomes δ+ and the halogen δ−.

q: Which C–X bond is the most polar?
x: Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, so the electronegativity difference, and hence the polarity, is greatest in the C–F bond.

q: For the same alkyl group, the correct order of reactivity of alkyl halides in nucleophilic substitution is:
x: Reactivity follows the ease of breaking the C–X bond. The C–I bond is the weakest, so iodoalkanes react fastest and fluoroalkanes slowest.

q: Iodoalkanes are more reactive than fluoroalkanes even though the C–F bond is more polar. This is because:
o: The C–I bond is the weakest and breaks most easily
Iodine is more electronegative than fluorine
The C–I bond is the shortest C–X bond
Fluoride ion is a better leaving group than iodide ion
x: Bond strength matters more than polarity here. The long C–I bond has the lowest bond energy, so it breaks most easily; the C–F bond is very strong.

q: The hybridisation of the carbon atom bonded to the halogen in an alkyl halide is:
x: In an alkyl halide the halogen-bearing carbon forms four single bonds in a tetrahedral arrangement, so it is sp³ hybridised.

q: Because of the polar C–X bond, the carbon atom bonded to the halogen in an alkyl halide is attacked mainly by:
x: The carbon is electron-deficient (δ+), so electron-rich species, nucleophiles, attack it. This is why alkyl halides typically undergo nucleophilic substitution.

q: Which of the following is the best leaving group in nucleophilic substitution reactions of alkyl halides?
x: I⁻ is large, stable and a very weak base, and the C–I bond is weak, so iodide leaves most easily. F⁻ and OH⁻ are poor leaving groups.

q: Alkyl halides are polar, yet they are almost insoluble in water. The main reason is that they:
o: Cannot form hydrogen bonds with water molecules
x: Dissolving would mean breaking water's hydrogen bonds, but alkyl halides cannot form hydrogen bonds with water to make up for it, so they stay largely undissolved.

q: Chloroethane and iodoethane are each warmed with aqueous NaOH under the same conditions. Which statement is correct?
o: Chloroethane reacts faster because the C–Cl bond is more polar
Both react at the same rate because the alkyl group is the same
Iodoethane reacts faster because the C–I bond is weaker
Neither reacts, because aqueous NaOH only causes elimination
x: With the same alkyl group, the rate depends on breaking the C–X bond. C–I is much weaker than C–Cl, so iodoethane is hydrolysed faster, even though C–Cl is more polar.

q: In the symbol SN2, the letters and number stand for:
x: SN2 means substitution nucleophilic bimolecular: two species (the alkyl halide and the nucleophile) take part in the single rate-determining step.

q: The rate equation for an SN2 reaction of an alkyl halide RX with OH⁻ is:
x: SN2 occurs in one step in which both RX and OH⁻ are involved, so the rate is first order in each and second order overall.

q: The rate equation for an SN1 reaction of an alkyl halide RX with a nucleophile Nu⁻ is:
x: In SN1 the slow step is ionisation of RX alone into a carbocation and X⁻. The nucleophile joins later in a fast step, so it does not appear in the rate equation.

q: The intermediate formed in an SN1 reaction is a:
o: Five-coordinate carbon that can be isolated
x: In the first, slow step the C–X bond breaks heterolytically, giving a carbocation and a halide ion; the nucleophile then attacks the carbocation.

q: In an SN2 reaction, the nucleophile attacks the carbon atom bearing the halogen:
o: From the side directly opposite the leaving halogen
From the same side as the leaving halogen
Only after the halogen has fully left
x: SN2 is a backside attack: the nucleophile approaches from the side opposite the leaving group, forming a transition state in which the bond to the nucleophile forms as the C–X bond breaks.

q: When an optically active alkyl halide reacts by the SN2 mechanism, the product has:
o: The same configuration as the reactant
x: Backside attack turns the other three groups over like an umbrella in the wind, so the configuration is inverted (Walden inversion).

q: An optically active alkyl halide that reacts by SN1 gives mainly a racemic mixture because:
o: The carbocation is planar and can be attacked from either face
The nucleophile always attacks from the back side
The reaction takes place in a single step
The halide ion attacks the product again
x: The sp² carbocation is flat, so the nucleophile can approach from either side with almost equal chance, giving both configurations and largely losing optical activity.

q: Which alkyl halide reacts fastest by the SN2 mechanism?
x: SN2 needs backside attack, which bulky groups hinder. The methyl halide has the least crowding, so it reacts fastest; the tertiary halide reacts slowest by SN2.

q: The correct order of reactivity of alkyl halides towards the SN1 mechanism is:
x: SN1 goes through a carbocation. Tertiary carbocations are the most stable (alkyl groups release electrons), so tertiary halides react fastest by SN1.

q: For an SN2 reaction, rate = k[RX][OH⁻]. If both [RX] and [OH⁻] are doubled, the rate becomes:
x: Rate is first order in each reactant: 2 × 2 = 4, so the rate increases four times. Doubling for only one reactant would give 2 times.

q: For alkyl halide P, doubling [OH⁻] at constant [RX] doubles the rate of substitution; for alkyl halide Q it has no effect on the rate. P and Q are most likely:
x: A rate that depends on [OH⁻] means SN2, typical of a primary halide like bromoethane. A rate independent of [OH⁻] means SN1, typical of a tertiary halide like 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

q: Heating an alkyl halide with a strong base to remove HX produces:
x: Removal of H and X from neighbouring carbons (dehydrohalogenation) creates a C=C double bond, giving an alkene.

q: Which reagent and condition convert bromoethane mainly into ethene?
x: Hot alcoholic KOH acts as a strong base and causes elimination of HBr to give ethene. Aqueous KOH mainly substitutes OH for Br, giving ethanol.

q: Which alkyl halide CANNOT give an alkene when heated with alcoholic KOH?
x: Elimination needs a hydrogen on a β-carbon next to the carbon carrying the halogen. Bromomethane has only one carbon, so no C=C can form and it gives substitution instead. The other three all have β-hydrogens.

q: The rate equation for an E2 reaction of an alkyl halide RX with a base B⁻ is:
x: E2 is a one-step, bimolecular process in which the base and the alkyl halide are both involved in the rate-determining step, so rate = k[RX][B⁻].

q: Which statement about the E2 mechanism is correct?
o: It proceeds through a carbocation intermediate
It occurs in a single step with no intermediate
Its rate depends only on the concentration of RX
It works only when there is no β-hydrogen
x: In E2 the base removes a β-H, the C=C forms and X⁻ leaves all at the same time in one concerted step, so there is no intermediate.

q: The E1 and SN1 reactions of the same alkyl halide have the same:
o: First, rate-determining step forming a carbocation
x: Both begin with slow ionisation of RX to a carbocation. In SN1 the carbocation then adds a nucleophile; in E1 it loses a β-proton to form an alkene.

q: Which alkyl halide most readily undergoes elimination by the E1 mechanism?
x: E1 goes through a carbocation, and the tertiary carbocation from (CH₃)₃CBr is the most stable. The other three are primary halides.

q: Which set of conditions favours elimination over substitution for 2-bromopropane?
o: Dilute aqueous NaOH at room temperature
Concentrated KOH in ethanol at high temperature
Dilute aqueous KOH with gentle warming
x: A strong, concentrated base in alcohol and a high temperature favour elimination (giving propene). Dilute aqueous base at lower temperature favours substitution (giving propan-2-ol).

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane is heated with concentrated alcoholic KOH. The main organic product is:
x: A tertiary halide with a strong base in hot alcohol mainly undergoes elimination: HBr is removed to give (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, 2-methylpropene. The alcohol would come from substitution in aqueous conditions.

q: 1-Bromopropane and 2-bromopropane are each heated with alcoholic KOH. The elimination products are:
x: From 1-bromopropane, H is removed from C-2; from 2-bromopropane, H is removed from C-1 or C-3. Either way the double bond is CH₃CH=CH₂, so both give propene. A ring such as cyclopropane cannot form by elimination of HBr.
